what_its_for: Crizotinib is a cancer medicine used to treat a certain type of lung cancer called non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). It works in patients whose cancer has a specific gene change (called ALK-positive or ROS1-positive). It works by blocking signals that tell cancer cells to grow and spread.
how_to_take: Swallow the capsule whole with a full glass of water. You can take it with or without food. Do not crush, chew, or open the capsules. If a capsule is broken or leaking, do not touch the powder inside — handle it carefully and wash your hands right away. Take it at the same times each day (usually morning and evening) to keep a steady level in your body.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 250 mg taken twice a day (every 12 hours). Your doctor may lower your dose if you have side effects. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and your next scheduled dose is more than 6 hours away, take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If your next dose is less than 6 hours away, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the capsules in their original container. Keep away from heat, light, and moisture. Keep out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused medicine safely — ask your pharmacist about a medicine take-back program near you.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit, grapefruit juice, and Seville oranges (found in some marmalades) — they can increase the amount of crizotinib in your blood and cause more side effects. Avoid St. John's Wort (an herbal supplement) as it can make crizotinib less effective. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel dizzy or have vision problems. Avoid starting new medications — including vitamins, herbal products, and over-the-counter drugs — without checking with your doctor or pharmacist first, as many medicines can interact with crizotinib.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: sudden shortness of breath or difficulty breathing; chest pain; fast or irregular heartbeat or fainting (signs of a heart rhythm problem); severe vision changes or vision loss; severe stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or yellowing of your skin or eyes (signs of liver problems); signs of a serious lung problem such as new or worsening cough or fever; swelling of your legs or feet; or signs of low blood cell counts such as unusual bruising, bleeding, or frequent infections. Also call your doctor if you have any side effect that is bothering you or not going away, including dizziness, nausea, diarrhea, constipation, or swelling.
when_it_works: Crizotinib starts working right away in your body, but it may take several weeks before you or your doctor can see or measure the effects on your cancer. Most patients begin to notice improvement within the first few months of treatment. It is important to keep taking it every day even if you feel well, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Crizotinib can harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant must use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 45 days after the last dose. Men with female partners who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 90 days after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking crizotinib and for at least 45 days after the last dose. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you have moderate to severe kidney or liver problems. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects and should be monitored closely. Children: Safety and effectiveness in children have not been fully established — use only if directed by a specialist.
